title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 22
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: One Price, Anywhere
passages.text:
A. Carrying messages is as old as writing, and organised systems of relay riders served rulers for millennia. What they served was the state's own correspondence. A private letter might travel by the same route if someone could be persuaded to carry it, but the network existed to move official information, and its speed was a military asset rather than a public service.

B. Opening these systems to the public produced an immediate pricing problem that shaped everything afterwards. Early public post was charged by distance and by the number of sheets, paid by the recipient on delivery, and the result was a system that was expensive, slow to settle and easy to defraud — a recipient could inspect the exterior, take the information encoded in the handwriting or the marks, and refuse to pay for a letter they had effectively already read.

C. The reform that resolved this was counter-intuitive and was resisted on the obvious grounds. A single low rate regardless of distance, prepaid by the sender with an adhesive stamp, appeared to undercharge the long journeys that cost most. Its defenders argued that the expensive part of carrying a letter was handling it at each end rather than moving it between, so distance-based pricing was charging for the cheap component and administering the charge cost more than it collected.

D. Volume settled the argument within a few years. Prepayment removed the delivery-time accounting that had consumed most of the labour, the low rate brought correspondence within reach of people who had never sent a letter, and traffic rose steeply enough that revenue recovered despite the lower rate per item. The model was copied internationally with unusual speed, and uniform pricing became the assumption rather than the innovation.

E. What followed was a set of obligations that no commercial operator would accept voluntarily. Delivery to remote addresses costs many times what delivery to dense ones does, and charging the same price everywhere means the profitable routes fund the unprofitable — an arrangement defensible as a public service and indefensible as a business, which is why it survives only where it is required by law rather than chosen.

F. That cross-subsidy is what electronic communication has undermined. The dense profitable traffic — bills, statements, personal correspondence — moved online first, leaving a network sized for a volume that no longer exists and still obliged to reach every address. Parcels have partly filled the gap and have brought competitors who serve the profitable areas without the obligation, which leaves the universal service holding the expensive remainder.

passages.title: Why Some Animals Last
passages.text:
Body size predicts lifespan across mammals with reasonable accuracy: a mouse lives a few years, an elephant several decades, and the relationship holds well enough to be a starting point. What makes the subject interesting is the animals that depart from it, because those departures are where the mechanisms show themselves.

Bats are the clearest exception. A bat of a mouse's mass can live thirty years or more, several times what its size predicts, and the difference is associated with flight. Species that fly — birds as well as bats — are consistently longer-lived than ground-dwelling animals of comparable size, and so are animals that live in trees, in burrows or with effective chemical defences. The pattern is not about metabolism, as was long assumed, but about how likely something is to be killed by causes outside itself — predation above all, though disease and starvation act in the same direction.

The reasoning behind this connection is one of the more elegant arguments in biology. Selection acts weakly on traits expressed late in life, because an animal that will probably be killed by a predator within two years gains nothing from machinery that would have protected it at twenty. Where predation is low, more individuals survive to older ages, late-life traits are exposed to selection, and longevity can evolve. Safety comes first and long life follows, not the other way round.

The same logic explains reproduction's relationship to lifespan. Animals under heavy predation are selected to reproduce early and abundantly, since a delayed reproductive strategy is worthless to an animal that will not survive to use it; animals that are relatively safe can afford slow development, few offspring and extended care. The pairing of high predation with early reproduction, and of safety with delay, is one of the strongest patterns in the field.

Some organisms decline so slowly that the usual pattern barely applies to them. Certain cold-water fish, some turtles and a number of trees show little measurable increase in mortality with age, which does not mean they cannot die but that being old does not itself make death more likely. These cases indicate that ageing as most animals experience it is not a physical inevitability so much as an outcome of how selection has been weighted.

Applying any of this to humans requires more caution than it usually receives. Our own longevity fits the pattern — large, slow-reproducing, historically well defended by group living — but the recent increase in human lifespan is a change in conditions rather than in biology, produced by sanitation, nutrition and medicine acting on the same organism. The species that have interested researchers most are studied for the mechanisms they might reveal, not because their arrangements are available to us.

passages.title: Where the Clothes Go
passages.text:
Clothing donated to charity in wealthy countries follows a route that most donors would not predict. A small proportion is sold in the collecting country's own shops; the great majority is sold by weight to sorting companies, graded, baled and exported, and arrives in markets several thousand kilometres away where it is sold at prices that undercut anything locally made. The transaction is commercial from the second step onward, and describing the whole chain as charity obscures more than it explains.

The trade is neither the disaster nor the benefit that its loudest advocates claim. It clothes large numbers of people cheaply and well, supports substantial employment in importing, sorting, repairing and retailing at the destination, and provides goods of a quality that local manufacturing at that price point does not match. These are real benefits accruing to real people, and they are routinely omitted from accounts written in the exporting countries.

The damage is equally real and falls on a different group. Domestic textile and garment industries in several importing countries contracted sharply during the decades when imports rose, and while other factors contributed — trade liberalisation, competition from new low-cost manufacturers, currency movements — the timing in several cases is difficult to attribute elsewhere. A country that loses its clothing industry loses the entry-level industrial employment that has historically begun industrialisation.

What has changed the calculation recently is quality rather than quantity. As garments have become cheaper and less durable, a rising share of what is exported is unsellable on arrival, and the cost of disposing of it falls on the importing country's waste system rather than on anyone in the chain who profited. Import restrictions introduced in several markets are frequently reported as protectionism, when the stated objection is as much about receiving waste as about competition.

The exporting side's accounting is where the misrepresentation concentrates. Collection is presented to donors as diversion from landfill, and material that is exported and then discarded is counted as diverted, because the counting stops at the port. A measure that records material leaving the country as material saved will report success regardless of what happens next, and the incentive to look further is absent for everyone the system rewards.

Reduction is the only response that addresses the cause, and it is the one no participant in the chain has an interest in. Fewer and better garments would shrink collection volumes, sorting revenues, export tonnages and the disposal burden simultaneously, which is a coherent policy and an unattractive one to every organisation currently funded by the flow.
